stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A county agricultural extension office wanted to estimate the percentage of all farmers in the county who plant cover crops. Staff surveyed 60 farmers who attended a free workshop on cover-crop methods, and 52 of them reported planting cover crops.
choices: The only flaw is the sample size; surveying 300 workshop attendees in the same way would fix the results.
The results may be biased because farmers at a cover-crop workshop are not a random sample of all county farmers.
Because 52 of the 60 farmers plant cover crops, most farmers in the county must also plant cover crops.
The results would be representative if staff had surveyed only farmers who did not attend the workshop.
explanation: The office wants to learn about all farmers in the county, but it sampled only farmers who chose to attend a cover-crop workshop. Those farmers are probably more interested in cover crops than farmers in general. Because the sample was not chosen at random from the whole population, the results may be biased.

A.why: You blamed the sample size. Surveying 300 attendees still samples only people drawn to a cover-crop event, so the bias stays. A bigger biased sample is still biased.

C.why: You treated a large majority in a biased sample as proof about the whole county. A lopsided result from an unrepresentative group says nothing reliable about everyone else.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Farmers who skipped the workshop are not a random sample of all farmers either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A folklorist wanted to estimate the percentage of adults in a river valley who can retell the local legend of the Drowned Bell. The folklorist placed a notice in the newsletter of the valley's storytelling society asking readers to reply and say whether they knew the legend. Of the 140 readers who replied, 126 said they could retell it.
choices: Because 126 of 140 respondents knew the legend, about 90% of all adults in the valley can retell it.
The only flaw is the sample size; getting 1,000 replies from newsletter readers would remove the problem.
The results would be representative if only adults who never read the newsletter had been surveyed.
The results may be biased because the respondents chose to reply and all read a storytelling newsletter.
explanation: The population is all adults in the valley. The sample, however, was self-selected from readers of a storytelling society's newsletter, a group especially likely to know local legends. The sample is not random, so the results may be biased.

A.why: You applied the 90% from a self-selected group of storytelling fans to every adult in the valley. A biased sample cannot support that generalization.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. More replies from the same newsletter would still be self-selected storytelling enthusiasts, so the bias would remain.

C.why: You swapped one special subgroup for its opposite. Adults who never read the newsletter are not a random sample of all valley adults either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city's transportation department wanted to know what percentage of city residents support spending $\$40$ million to widen the Harlow Street Bridge. Surveyors stopped 250 drivers who were waiting in traffic on the bridge during the morning rush hour, and 210 of them supported the project.
choices: The results may be biased because drivers stuck on the bridge are not a random sample of all city residents.
The results show that $84\%$ of all city residents support spending $\$40$ million to widen the bridge.
The main flaw is the sample size; stopping 1,000 drivers on the bridge would make the results reliable.
The results would be representative if surveyors had asked only residents who never use the bridge.
explanation: The department wants the opinion of all city residents, but it surveyed only drivers stuck in traffic on the bridge. That group has a direct stake in widening it. Because the sample was convenient and not random, the results may be biased.

B.why: You computed $\frac{210}{250} = 84\%$ correctly but applied it to every resident. A sample drawn from frustrated bridge drivers cannot be generalized to the whole city.

C.why: You blamed the sample size. Stopping 1,000 drivers on the same bridge would still sample only people with a stake in the project.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Residents who never use the bridge are not a random sample of the city either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A regional water utility wanted to estimate the percentage of its customer households that had low water pressure at least once last month. The utility posted an optional online form inviting customers to report whether they had experienced low pressure. Of the 300 households that chose to submit the form, 240 reported low pressure.
choices: Because 240 of 300 households reported low pressure, $80\%$ of all customer households had low pressure.
The results would be reliable if the utility had collected 3,000 forms in exactly the same way.
The results may be biased because households with pressure problems were more likely to choose to respond.
The results would be representative if only households with no pressure problems had been surveyed.
explanation: The utility wants to learn about all of its customer households, but the households that answered chose to answer. Customers who had pressure problems have a reason to respond, so the sample is self-selected and the results may be biased.

A.why: You applied the $80\%$ from a self-selected group to every customer household. Volunteers with complaints overstate how common the problem is.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. Collecting 3,000 forms the same way still lets the households with problems choose themselves, so the bias stays.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Surveying only households without problems would be biased in the other direction.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city planning office wanted to estimate the percentage of all city residents who favor replacing one lane of downtown street parking with a protected bike lane. A planner surveyed 80 customers at a downtown bicycle repair shop, and 72 of them favored the bike lane.
choices: The results may be biased because bike shop customers are not a random sample of all city residents.
Because 72 of the 80 customers favored the bike lane, $90\%$ of all city residents favor it.
The only flaw is the small sample; surveying 400 bike shop customers would make the results reliable.
The results would be representative if the planner had surveyed only drivers at a downtown parking garage.
explanation: The office wants the views of all city residents, but the planner surveyed only bicycle repair customers, who are likely to favor bike lanes. The sample is convenient and not random, so the results may be biased.

B.why: You treated the $90\%$ majority among cyclists as a fact about every resident. A biased sample cannot be generalized to the whole city.

C.why: You blamed the sample size. Surveying 400 bike shop customers still samples only cyclists, so a larger sample would not remove the bias.

D.why: You swapped cyclists for drivers. Drivers at a parking garage have the opposite stake, so they are also not a random sample of residents.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A music researcher wanted to estimate the percentage of adults in a city who listen to classical music at least once a week. The researcher surveyed 150 people as they left a symphony orchestra concert, and 135 of them said they listen to classical music at least once a week.
choices: Because 135 of 150 people surveyed listen weekly, $90\%$ of the city's adults listen to classical music weekly.
The only flaw is the sample size; surveying 600 people leaving the concert would make the results reliable.
The results may be biased because concertgoers at a symphony are not a random sample of the city's adults.
The results would be representative if the researcher had surveyed only people leaving a rock concert.
explanation: The population is all adults in the city, but the sample came from a symphony audience, a group that is especially likely to listen to classical music. The sample was not randomly chosen, so the results may be biased.

A.why: You applied the $90\%$ from a symphony audience to every adult in the city. A clear majority in a biased sample proves nothing about the population.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. Surveying 600 symphony concertgoers is still surveying only symphony concertgoers, so the bias remains.

D.why: You swapped one special audience for another. People leaving a rock concert are not a random sample of the city's adults either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: Marine biologists wanted to estimate the mean shell width of all blue crabs in a large bay. For convenience, they trapped 200 crabs in the shallow cove beside their laboratory dock, where the water is warmer than in most of the bay. The mean shell width of the trapped crabs was 14 centimeters.
choices: Because the sample mean was 14 centimeters, the mean shell width of all crabs in the bay is 14 centimeters.
The only flaw is the sample size; trapping 800 crabs in the same cove would make the estimate reliable.
The estimate would be representative if crabs had been trapped only in the bay's coldest, deepest water.
The estimate may be biased because crabs from one convenient cove are not a random sample from the bay.
explanation: The biologists want to learn about all blue crabs in the bay, but they trapped crabs in only one convenient cove with unusual conditions. That is not a random sample from the whole bay, so the estimate may be biased.

A.why: You treated the cove's sample mean as the exact mean for the whole bay. Crabs from one warm cove cannot stand in for the bay's entire crab population.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. Trapping 800 crabs in the same cove repeats the same convenience sampling, so the bias stays.

C.why: You swapped one unusual location for the opposite extreme. Crabs from only the coldest, deepest water are not a random sample of the bay either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A steel mill wanted to estimate the percentage of all beams it produced last month that contain internal cracks. Engineers tested the 50 beams from last month that customers had returned with complaints, and 35 of those beams contained internal cracks.
choices: Because 35 of the 50 tested beams had cracks, $70\%$ of all beams produced last month contain cracks.
The results may be biased because returned beams are not a random sample of all beams produced last month.
The only flaw is the sample size; testing 500 returned beams would make the estimate reliable.
The estimate would be representative if engineers had tested only beams that no customer complained about.
explanation: The mill wants to learn about every beam it produced last month, but the engineers tested only beams that customers returned with complaints. Those beams are especially likely to be defective. The sample is not random, so the estimate may be biased.

A.why: You applied the $70\%$ from complaint returns to the whole month's production. Beams sent back because of problems will overstate the defect rate.

C.why: You blamed the sample size. Testing more returned beams still samples only beams that customers complained about, so the bias stays.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Beams with no complaints would understate the defect rate, so they are not a random sample either.
